en: Ez kara, khan of the Manchus,
Will find some way to deal with me!
Six thousand Chinese, countless officers,
And Alakoo's Kongurbay
Will raid and slaughter my village!
Ez kara, khan of the Manchus,
Will find some way to deal with me!
Will the Kyrgyz be carried off as booty?!
Will the Chinese bring about my end?!
Digging my pit deep,
Starting strife in the dark night,
The Chinese emperor's people made ready,
And showed me calamity!”
Muttering as he spoke his last wishes,
Grieving as he walked, crying out,
Your father took a pole,
Unable to strike the renowned Chinese giant.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Your father, once happy Manas,
Could not find his bearings.
God's sun in heaven grew overcast.
Sixty cares came upon his head at once.
Holding the pole, he begged;
Your hero stammered his profession of faith.
“Akkula, whom I rode without rest—
Has he come to rest this year?
These dear people, robbed of peace—
Did the Chinese come in secret
And silence them without a sound?
I shall take an enemy down with me,” he said.
Your blessed father strode about.
As though a bullet would wipe him clean away,
Your barefoot father lumbered along.
As he was about to reach the foremost camel,
About to plunge among them,
As his appointed death drew near,
Alakoo's Kongurbay
Was about to give a piercing shout,
About to bind him alive.
Your father's Akkula,
The great steed brought to full condition,
Could race a flying bird—
Such had Akkula become.
The belly flesh from which kazy is cut
Clung to his lower ribs.
Akkula, brought to full condition—
I was alarmed by this turn of events.
So that the foolish lord might ride,
Without resentment I saddled him.
Ak kangky, made by Almambet,
The broad-pommel saddle that fitted Akkula,
Its front bow of white gold,
Its rear bow of pure silver,
Broad iron on both sides—
Ak kangky, ridden into spear battle,
Fit for your father to ride,
I saddled in angry haste.
“Your father neglected me”—
In the end I bore no grudge for that.
Pulling his belly girth tight,
That Akkula standing there,
Shortening his crupper,
Having him covered with bulletproof armor,
His lead rope in okoro braid
I had fastened a little longer,
And sent him racing, roused to fury.
Steel bullets in white saddlebags,
Six poods in all.
When her heart burned, your mother—
I threw them onto Ak kangky.
I walked softly, pleading,
Ak kelte and Akolpok,
Holding both equally in my hands.
I, your mother, set aside my resentment,
And begged your father.
The great lead rope in okoro braid
I put tightly around my neck.
Ak kelte and Akolpok,
Syr nayza and Akkula,
With Zulpukor, these five,
I, your mother, setting aside my resentment,
Presented to your father:
“Here is the royal city,
If you believe those old words,
My king, if you would cut off my head, here I am!
Here are the honored Kyrgyz people;
If you would spill my blood, here I am!
If you would bind me, here are my hands;
If you would dig deep, here is the pit;
If you would listen, generous lord, here are my words;
If you would gouge them out, here are my eyes!
Sever it—here is my fragile life!
If you would ride, here is the steed Akkula!
Can one who listens to gossip prosper?
Believing a troublemaker—
My king, can a warrior like you do this?
At the seething imperial Chinese,
Look, sultan panther!
You have courage but no sense.
Can you go in unarmored?!
You have no garden built in Talas;
Warrior, this is no time to strut about.
You have no garden planted in Keng-Kol;
Warrior, this is no time to lie stretched at ease.
When you were ravaging the Afghans,
Akylay, daughter of Khan Shooruk—
Warrior, the wife you seized—
Holding her dear,
My fierce one, your reason has gone astray.
The royal Chinese are a burning bullet.
My king, can one prosper going in stocking-footed?
Preparing all your equipment—
Could that wife be like me?
A warm bed, sweet sleep,
You lie close together, playing.
With no care for anything,
Should a wife be like that?
If you play, my lord, you will die;
You will see the other world's face.
Taking offense at groundless words,
You keep speaking roughly to people.
I have spent so much strength;
My king, you have spilled so much of my blood.
You have wasted so much of your strength.
Akylay, that childish wife—
Akylay has become your kin.
Believing the slave Kyrgylchal,
You left me a neglected wife for six months.
I brought you as an offering
That fleet steed of yours, like Akkula.
Bulletproof when entering battle,
Here is Akolpok; put it on and enter.
Exceptionally sharp, the iron Almabash,
Making no distinction between far and near,
Not failing for sixty days—
The cherished Ak kelte,
Sling it over your shoulder,
Sparing nothing, the time has come;
My sultan, charge into the enemy ahead!
Long was I a neglected wife,
Without rest by day,
Without sleep by night.
‘It is needed against the foe we fight,’ I thought.
That mighty weapon, Syr nayza,
I give you as a gift—take it.
The emperor's people are a grievous affliction;
My sultan, charge and wage war!
When drawn from its sheath with a shout,
It never goes idly without drinking blood;
Unless it drinks its fill of blood,
It never returns to its sheath.
I give you Zulpukor—take it.
Against Kongurbay, khan of the Chinese,
Fight with all your might.
The great Kyrgyz people, rich in customs—
If you can, my sultan,
Rescue them!”
Mounting him on Akkula,
Clothing him in Akolpok,
Showed him what she had gathered.
I kindled his extinguished fire,
Revived his deadened spirit,
Joined what had broken,
Gathered what had scattered.
Your foolish father's—
Without resentment, wretched me,
I planted and made a garden.
A good wife makes a good husband—
Thus I made your father a khan.
I made my great head a banner;
Woman though I was, I made myself a warrior.
Your father, Manas the Lion,
Who could not drink his fill of blood,
Upon the mortals of humankind
Never ceased to bring distress.
Instead of charging into the enemy,
Your father stood pleading.
Your father let himself go,
Begging wretched me:
“Your father's grave, my lady!
Those currant-like eyes of yours!
Let me devote myself to you,
To your black eyes, clear as glass;
I can only turn about you in devotion!
My poor dear, who opens my life's bazaar!
My sweet-tongued nightingale,
My dear one, always my support,
If my khanly head survives,
I shall not raise my whip and strike.
Snarling and quarreling,
I shall not say this and that against you.
While my dear head remains,
I shall not, even if a flood engulfs me.
What you have done,
My lady, I shall never gainsay!
Kongurbay, khan of the tonsured ones,
Was about to seize me in my shirt;
Ez kara, khan of the Manchus,
Was about to slaughter me as a sacrifice;
Red-whip Shypshaydar,
Gathering his giants and warriors,
Was about to seize me alive…”
Your father said this with joy,
Then brought slaughter upon the Chinese.
The dear Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
When clear dawn broke,
He rescued them.
The gray belt descended from heaven,
Girded tightly about his waist,
Against seventy thousand Chinese,
Your father plunged alone to attack.
Roaring in fury,
Sounding the battle cry, “Ystan!”
With a cotton belt and broad boots,
Kongurbay, khan of the tonsured ones,
Was a skilled spearman,
A mighty man who knew the enemy's stratagems.
Six thousand Chinese, countless officers,
Their elder Kongurbay,
At your father, the lion himself,
Thrust their spears together.
Makil, huge as Opol-Too,
At your most excellent father Manas,
Thrust his spear from below.
The mighty ones clad in coats,
Around your hapless father Manas,
Were standing in a ring.
I, your fierce mother,
Was sorely troubled in heart;
Tears poured from my eyes.
“Let me die instead of living on.
To the generous lord to whom I was pledged,
Woman though I am, poor soul,
Let me be a support,”
I said then, poor soul.
My splendid hair, thick as a girth,
I bound tightly atop my head.
A helmet like blue iron
I put over my head.
A steed among horses, a sleek stallion,
The black horse with a white blaze—
I saddled him firmly and mounted.
“If I live and do not die,
What wish shall I achieve?
Rather, poor soul,
For my blood-shedding, fierce Manas,
Let me sacrifice myself!”
Before I could reach him,
His eyes narrowed like a lion's.
Upon the lion himself,
Six thousand spears struck at once.
Your father rang out, unheeding;
All except Kongurbay
He counted as nothing.
His eyes as vast as a lake's bed,
Grappling with my fierce one,
